Content:
The addition law for probability states that if we have two events [MATH: A] and [MATH: B,] the probability of their union equals the sum of their individual probabilities minus the probability of their intersection.

Content:
We can state the addition law mathematically as follows:

Content:
[MATH: P(A\cup B)= P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)]

Content:
There's some nice intuition behind this law.

Content:
- By adding [MATH: P(A)] to [MATH: P(B)] to work out [MATH: P(A \cup B),] we count the intersection [MATH: P(A \cap B)] twice.
- So, to get the correct formula for [MATH: P(A\cup B),] we need to subtract one of the intersections.

Content:
Let's look at a concrete example.

items.title: Applying the Addition Law in Context

sections.normalized_html: An icosahedral ([MATH: 20]-sided) die is rolled. What is the probability of getting a prime number or an even number?
sections.readable_text: An icosahedral ([MATH: 20]-sided) die is rolled. What is the probability of getting a prime number or an even number?

sections.normalized_html:
Let us call [MATH: R] the event "We get a prime number", and [MATH: E] the event "We get an even number". Then the probability of getting a prime number or an even number is [MATH: P(R \cup E),] and we can apply the addition law:

[MATH: P(R∪E)|= P(R) + P(E) − P(R∩E)]

First, let's find [MATH: P(R),] [MATH: P(E),] and [MATH: P(R \cap E).]

  • There are [MATH: 8] prime numbers among the [MATH: 20] faces of the die ([MATH: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19]), so we have [MATH: P(R) = \frac{8}{20}.]

  • There are [MATH: 10] even numbers among the [MATH: 20] faces of the die, so we have [MATH: P(E) = \frac{10}{20}.]

  • There is only a single number, [MATH: 2,] that is both prime and even. So, we have [MATH: P(R \cap E) = \frac{1}{20}.]

Therefore, applying the addition law, we have

[MATH: P(R∪E)|= P(R) + P(E) − P(R∩E); = (8)/(20) + (10)/(20) − (1)/(20); = (17)/(20).]

sections.normalized_html:
A card is drawn at random from a standard [MATH: 52]-card deck. What is the probability of drawing a card labeled with an odd number or a black card?

Hint: An ace card is not considered to be an odd-numbered card.
sections.readable_text:
A card is drawn at random from a standard [MATH: 52]-card deck. What is the probability of drawing a card labeled with an odd number or a black card?

Hint: An ace card is not considered to be an odd-numbered card.

sections.normalized_html:
Let's call [MATH: O] the event "a card labeled with an odd number is selected" and [MATH: B] the event "a black card is selected."

The required probability is [MATH: P(O \cup B),] which we can find using the addition law: [MATH: P(O \cup B) = P(O) + P(B) - P(O \cap B)]

Let's find [MATH: P(O)] and [MATH: P(B).]

  • There are [MATH: 4] odd-numbered cards in each suit in a standard deck ([MATH: 3,5,7,9]), and there are [MATH: 4] suits in total. So, we have [MATH: P(O) = \dfrac{4\cdot 4}{52} =\dfrac{16}{52} = \dfrac{4}{13}.]

  • There are [MATH: 26] black cards in a standard deck. So, we have [MATH: P(B) = \dfrac{26}{52} = \dfrac{1}{2}.]

Moreover, since [MATH: O] and [MATH: B] are independent, we have [MATH: P(O∩B)|= P(O) ⋅ P(B); = (4)/(13) ⋅ (1)/(2); = (2)/(13).]

Finally, substituting all of the known information into the addition law, we get [MATH: P(O∪B)|= P(O) + P(B) − P(O∩B); = (4)/(13) + (1)/(2) − (2)/(13); = (17)/(26).]

[MATH: P(R∪E)|= P(R) + P(E) − P(R∩E)]

First, let's find [MATH: P(R),] [MATH: P(E),] and [MATH: P(R \cap E).]

- There are [MATH: 8] prime numbers among the [MATH: 20] faces of the die ([MATH: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19]), so we have

[MATH: P(E) = \frac{10}{20}.]
- There is only a single number, [MATH: 2,] that is both prime and even. So, we have
[MATH: P(R \cap E) = \frac{1}{20}.]

Therefore, applying the addition law, we have

[MATH: P(R∪E)|= P(R) + P(E) − P(R∩E); = (8)/(20) + (10)/(20) − (1)/(20); = (17)/(20).]

The required probability is [MATH: P(O \cup B),] which we can find using the addition law:
[MATH: P(O \cup B) = P(O) + P(B) - P(O \cap B)]

Let's find [MATH: P(O)] and [MATH: P(B).]

- There are [MATH: 4] odd-numbered cards in each suit in a standard deck ([MATH: 3,5,7,9]), and there are [MATH: 4] suits in total. So, we have
[MATH: P(O) = \dfrac{4\cdot 4}{52} =\dfrac{16}{52} = \dfrac{4}{13}.]
- There are [MATH: 26] black cards in a standard deck. So, we have
[MATH: P(B) = \dfrac{26}{52} = \dfrac{1}{2}.]

Moreover, since [MATH: O] and [MATH: B] are independent, we have
[MATH: P(O∩B)|= P(O) ⋅ P(B); = (4)/(13) ⋅ (1)/(2); = (2)/(13).]

Finally, substituting all of the known information into the addition law, we get
[MATH: P(O∪B)|= P(O) + P(B) − P(O∩B); = (4)/(13) + (1)/(2) − (2)/(13); = (17)/(26).]
